blocks.title: AI & Me
blocks.description: Find the AI already in your day, distinguish it from fixed-rule software, and start asking who it helps and who it might harm.
blocks.mission: Create a one-page AI in My Day map showing at least five systems that use AI. For two of them, show INPUT → AI ACTION → OUTPUT → BENEFIT → RISK.
route: Experience Lab: draw for the AI
blocks.final: Draw-for-the-AI lab evidence, AI in My Day map, human-vs-AI comparison, and exit reflection.

sessions.title: AI or not?
sessions.intro: Vote before you get a definition, then use three questions to revisit your first instinct.

study.title: Three questions that help
body: There is no perfect one-line test for AI. A useful starting point is to ask whether a system uses data, finds or generates patterns, and adapts or predicts rather than only following one fixed rule.
Automation is not automatically AI. A timer and a calculator can be useful software while still following explicit rules written by people.
Modern products can mix ordinary software and AI, so some examples are genuinely borderline. Your job is to explain the evidence for your choice, not to force everything into one box.
study.example: A timer follows a fixed setting. A spam filter can use patterns from earlier examples to estimate whether a new message is spam.

activity.title: Hook: AI or not?
activity.instructions: Choose AI, not AI, or unsure for each. You can change your answers after reading the study material.

sessions.reflection: Choose one example and explain what evidence makes you think it contains AI, rather than only a fixed rule.

sessions.title: Can AI recognise what I draw?
sessions.intro: Predict what an AI will do, watch what it actually does, then change your input and see what changes.

study.title: Recognition is pattern-matching, not understanding
body: A recognition system compares your input with patterns learned from millions of earlier examples. It does not know what a cat is; it knows what most people's cat drawings looked like.
That is why it can guess a rough sketch in seconds and still fail on an unusual, tilted or partial drawing. The failure tells you what the training data looked like.
A good experiment records the prediction before the result, the result itself, one failure, and what changed when the input changed.
study.example: Draw a bicycle with two circles and a bar and the AI may guess it instantly. Draw the same bicycle from the front and it may say 'glasses'.

activity.title: Experience Lab: draw for the AI
activity.instructions: Read the safety notice, open the tool, play one round of six drawings, then record what actually happened. If the tool is blocked or offline, use the fallback.
privacy: Quick, Draw! keeps drawings for public research. Draw only the simple object it asks for; never write words, names, faces or personal details.
Use objects and drawings, never faces, names or anything that identifies you or another person.
Do not sign in or create an account. These tools work without one.
Nothing you type into this portal is sent to the external tool; record your evidence here, not there.
steps: Before you start, predict which of the six words the AI will get right and which it will miss.
Play one round. Watch which guesses appear while you are still drawing.
Note one drawing it got wrong or took longest on, and what it guessed instead.
Redraw that object a different way (angle, size, detail). Did the guess change?
Record your evidence below in your own words.

fallback.title: Tool blocked or offline?
steps: Pair up. One person is the AI: they may only guess from the lines drawn so far, no questions allowed.
The other draws six objects from the Student Book list, 20 seconds each.
Record which were guessed, which failed, and what the 'AI' said instead.
Redraw one failed object differently and see whether the guess changes.

fields: My prediction before I started…
What the AI actually did…
One unexpected result or failure…
What changed when I changed my drawing…
My evidence (which objects, how many guessed, how quickly)…

sessions.reflection: What does the AI's mistake tell you about the examples it learned from, and why is that different from how a person recognises things?

sessions.title: AI in My Day
sessions.intro: Map a normal day and make the hidden input-to-output chain visible.

study.title: The influence lens
body: To understand an AI system, follow the chain: INPUT is the data that goes in; AI ACTION is the pattern-finding, ranking, prediction or generation; OUTPUT is what comes out.
Then ask about consequence. BENEFIT asks who gains. RISK asks what could go wrong. A final stakeholder question is: who might be affected besides you?
Recommendation systems can create feedback loops: what you click today can influence what you see tomorrow, which can influence what you click next.
study.example: Listening history → finds patterns in what similar people play → playlist → new music discovery → risk of repeatedly hearing more of the same.

activity.title: Build your AI in My Day map
activity.instructions: Add five systems from waking up to going to sleep. Complete the full chain for at least two rows.

sessions.reflection: Which system on your map has the most influence over you, and who else could be affected by its output?

sessions.title: Human vs AI
sessions.intro: Compare strengths without assuming either humans or AI are automatically better.

study.title: Ability is not the same as responsibility
body: Current AI systems can be fast at pattern-heavy tasks, generating alternatives, sorting large amounts of information and producing fluent output.
Humans bring lived context, values, responsibility, judgement about consequences and the ability to decide when a task should not be automated.
A useful comparison asks not only who can do a task, but who should make the final decision and who is accountable when something goes wrong.
study.example: A recommendation model can rank thousands of songs quickly. A person can decide whether the recommendation is appropriate for a particular situation and can reject it.

activity.title: Human vs AI comparison + micro-debate
activity.instructions: Write your own comparison, then take a position on: ‘Recommendation algorithms mostly help us.’
fields: Humans are better at…
Current AI systems are better at…
My position on the debate…
One example that supports my position…

sessions.reflection: Did your position move after considering another point of view? Explain what changed or why it did not.

sessions.title: Exit reflection
sessions.intro: Finish Chapter 1 by putting the idea into your own words.

study.title: Myth-busters to remember
body: AI does not simply mean robots; most AI you meet is software such as ranking, filtering, prediction or generation.
Not every computer program is AI. Fixed-rule software and learned systems can exist side by side.
Using AI does not make a system objective. Data and design choices come from people and can still produce unfair outcomes.
study.example: A system can be consistent every time and still be consistently unfair.

activity.title: Chapter evidence check
activity.instructions: Confirm the three pieces of portfolio evidence you now have.
fields: One thing I now notice about AI…
One question I want answered later…

sessions.reflection: In two or three sentences, explain the biggest idea you are taking from AI & Me.

blocks.title: Teaching a Machine
blocks.description: Teach a computer to tell two objects apart, then deliberately find where it fails and improve it with evidence.
blocks.mission: Train a two-class model, produce a 10-row test log and confusion matrix, find one failure pattern, improve the model, and show before-and-after evidence.
blocks.final: Dataset plan, v1 test log and accuracy, confusion matrix, shortcut-learning observation, v2 improvement note, and reflection.

sessions.title: Be the classifier
sessions.intro: Try written rules first so you can see why machine learning uses labelled examples.

study.title: From rules to learning
body: Supervised learning teaches a model with examples that already have the right class label attached.
A feature is something measurable about an example, such as shape, edges, brightness or proportions. The model learns statistical patterns in those features; nobody types every rule into it.
Training data are the labelled examples used for learning. Test data must be genuinely different, otherwise you are mostly testing memory rather than generalisation.
study.example: Instead of writing ‘cups have handles’, show the model many labelled cup and bottle examples and let it learn separating patterns.

activity.title: Human classifier
activity.instructions: Write rules another group could use to tell two objects apart, then note an unusual example that breaks one rule.
fields: My two classes
Rule 1
Rule 2
An unusual example that breaks a rule

sessions.reflection: Why do fixed written rules run out quickly when examples become unusual?

sessions.title: Build model v1
sessions.intro: Collect balanced, varied examples and record the conditions before you train.

study.title: Training data shapes the model
body: A balanced dataset contains roughly similar numbers of examples for each class.
A varied dataset includes realistic differences in lighting, angle, distance and background.
More examples are not automatically better if they all repeat the same accidental pattern.
study.example: Twenty cup photos from one angle on one desk can teach less than twenty varied cup photos across different angles and backgrounds.

activity.title: Experience Lab: train CUP vs BOTTLE
activity.instructions: Read the safety notice, open the tool, train model v1, then record your classes, example counts, conditions and one predicted weak case. If the tool is blocked, use the fallback.
privacy: Point the camera only at safe objects on a desk. Keep faces, other people and anything with a name or address out of every image.
Use objects and drawings, never faces, names or anything that identifies you or another person.
Do not sign in or create an account. These tools work without one.
Nothing you type into this portal is sent to the external tool; record your evidence here, not there.
steps: Create two safe object classes.
Collect a balanced set of examples.
Vary angle, distance, lighting and background.
Train model v1.
Record the case you expect to be weakest.

steps: Download the training set v1 below and upload its cup and bottle folders to the tool instead of using a camera. If the tool itself is blocked: print or sketch 20 cards, 10 per class.
Sort them into two piles by one visible rule you choose, such as 'has a handle'. That rule is your model v1.
Record the rule, how many cards each pile has, and which card you expect the rule to get wrong.
Keep the cards: you will test them in the next session.

Conditions I varied (angle, distance, light, background)…
The case I predict will be weakest, and why…
What happened when I trained v1…

downloads.label: Cup vs Bottle training set v1 (zip, 40 images)
downloads.note: Drawn shapes, 20 per class, varied colour, size, position and background. Upload the cup and bottle folders as your two classes if you have no camera.

sessions.reflection: What did you vary in the training examples, and why should that matter?

sessions.title: Break it and log the evidence
sessions.intro: Your goal is to find failures, not to make the model look good.

study.title: Testing and accuracy
body: Useful testing uses unseen examples: different objects, new angles, unusual lighting, cluttered backgrounds or partial views.
Accuracy is correct predictions divided by total predictions. It is useful, but it does not explain which kinds of errors occurred.
A model that never fails in your tests may simply mean the tests are too easy.
study.example: 8 correct predictions out of 10 tests gives 80% accuracy. The two failures are evidence worth investigating.

activity.title: Model test log
activity.instructions: Record at least 10 tests: actual class, prediction and an observation about angle, light, background or another condition.

downloads.label: Unseen test set (zip, 10 images + labels)
downloads.note: Test each image, record the prediction, then check labels.csv.

downloads.label: Test log template (CSV)
downloads.note: Same columns as the on-screen log.

sessions.reflection: Which test condition produced the most interesting failure, and what was different from your training data?

sessions.title: Read the confusion matrix
sessions.intro: Accuracy hides which mistakes happened. The confusion matrix separates them.

study.title: Which error matters?
body: A confusion matrix compares what was actually true with what the model predicted.
Correct predictions sit where actual and predicted classes match; the other cells show the two directions of error.
Which error matters more depends on the job. The consequences of a spam-filter mistake and a medical-screening mistake are not the same.
study.example: Two models can have the same overall accuracy but make different kinds of mistakes, so the matrix can reveal a weakness that accuracy hides.

activity.title: Build your 2×2 matrix
activity.instructions: Enter the counts from the same test log and calculate accuracy.

downloads.label: Confusion matrix template (CSV)
downloads.note: Four cells plus the accuracy formula.

sessions.reflection: Why might high accuracy on its own still hide an important weakness?

sessions.title: The shortcut experiment
sessions.intro: Deliberately build a flawed dataset so you can see shortcut learning happen.

study.title: Shortcut learning and bias
body: A model searches for statistical patterns that reduce error. It does not automatically know which pattern humans intended it to learn.
Shortcut learning happens when the model relies on an easy accidental clue, such as background colour, instead of the object itself.
Bias can enter through data even when nobody deliberately writes an unfair rule.
study.example: If cups are almost always photographed on a light background and bottles on a dark one, the model may learn background colour. Swap backgrounds and the prediction can collapse.

activity.title: Background trap
activity.instructions: Create the flawed background correlation, test with backgrounds swapped, and record what happened.
fields: How I created the shortcut
What happened when I swapped backgrounds
What pattern the model may have learned

downloads.label: Shortcut trap set (zip)
downloads.note: Every training cup is on a dark background, every bottle on a light one. The test folder swaps them. Train on train/, test on test/, and watch what the model actually learned.

sessions.reflection: Give another accidental shortcut an image model could learn from a badly designed dataset.

sessions.title: Improve model v2
sessions.intro: Use the failure evidence to make targeted changes, then test again fairly.

study.title: Improve with evidence
body: Propose changes that address the failure you actually observed: more variety, better balance, mixed backgrounds, clearer labels or additional representative examples.
Where possible, retest v2 using the same test set as v1 so the comparison is fair.
A better model is supported by before-and-after evidence, not by confidence or a single successful example.
study.example: If dark backgrounds caused cup errors, add both classes on light and dark backgrounds, retrain, then repeat the same background challenge.

activity.title: Model v2 improvement note
activity.instructions: Record at least two changes and what happened when you retested.
fields: Change 1 and why
Change 2 and why
What improved
What is still uncertain

downloads.label: Training set v2 (zip, 40 images)
downloads.note: Both classes on both background types. Train v2 here, then re-run the shortcut trap test folder.

sessions.reflection: Which change had the strongest evidence of improvement, or what would you test next?

sessions.title: Compare and reflect
sessions.intro: Finish with numbers plus examples, and be explicit about what is still uncertain.

study.title: A trustworthy evaluation is more than one score
body: Present what changed from v1 to v2, what improved, and what remains uncertain.
A confusion matrix shows error types that overall accuracy can hide.
Variety and balance can matter more than simply collecting a larger volume of near-identical examples.
study.example: If v2 scores better on your tests but you cannot explain why, say so. Uncertainty is part of honest evaluation.

activity.title: Before-and-after evidence
activity.instructions: Summarise your model experiment for the portfolio.
fields: v1 accuracy / main weakness
v2 accuracy / main improvement
One limitation that remains

sessions.reflection: Why might ‘high accuracy’ on its own not mean a model can be trusted? Use your own shortcut result or test evidence.

lab.title: Train and break a model
lab.summary: You train a real classifier, test it on unseen examples, break it on purpose, diagnose the shortcut it learned, and prove your v2 is better.

blocks.title: Data Detective
blocks.description: Investigate the data behind a school app: where each field came from, what is wrong with it, who it could harm, and what a model trained on it would learn.
blocks.mission: Investigate a flawed dataset for a school app, fix or flag every problem you find, and publish a Responsible Data Card that says what the data can and cannot be trusted for.
route: Hook: where did this data come from?
blocks.final: Data-source sort, first look at the dataset, audit findings table, cleaning and collection plan, and a Responsible Data Card.

sessions.title: Volunteered, observed, inferred
sessions.intro: Sort eight pieces of data by how they were obtained, before you learn why the difference matters.

study.title: Three ways data gets into a system
body: Volunteered data is what a person knowingly gives: the club they tick on a form, the phone number they type in, the interests they list. They know it exists, and they usually expect it to be used for the reason they gave it.

Observed data is collected by watching behaviour: which pages someone opens, at what time, for how long, on which device. Nobody typed it in, so most people never see it and cannot easily check whether it is accurate.

Inferred data is a guess the system makes from the other two, such as 'probably interested in sport' or 'likely low income'. It was never given and never directly observed; it is a prediction about a person, and predictions can be wrong, unfair, or both. The more sensitive the guess, the more careful you have to be about whether it should exist at all.
study.example: A school app asks you to tick Coding as your club (volunteered), notices you open the timetable every morning at 8:05 (observed), and guesses that your family probably cannot afford the trip (inferred). Only the first one is something you actually said.

activity.title: Hook: where did this data come from?
activity.instructions: For each item, choose whether a school app would have it because the student volunteered it, because the app observed it, or because the app inferred it. Change your answers after reading the study material if you want to.
items: Club choice ticked on a form
Pages visited in the school app
Parent phone number typed at sign-up
Time of day the app is usually opened
Interests typed into the sign-up form
How many times the timetable was checked this week

sessions.reflection: Pick one inferred item and explain who could be harmed if the guess is wrong, and who could be harmed even if it is right.

sessions.title: Meet the dataset
sessions.intro: You are the junior analyst. Open the club sign-up dataset the school wants to feed into a new app and take a first, careful look.

study.title: Read a dataset before you trust it
body: A dataset is a table: each row is one record, usually one person or one event, and each column is one field. Before doing anything clever with it, an analyst asks four plain questions: what is this for, who is in it, what does each column mean, and how did each value get here?

Two habits make the difference between a quick glance and a real inspection. First, read the column names and ask which ones the stated purpose actually needs. Second, scroll the values, not just the first few rows: strange formats, blanks and repeats hide in the middle.

Keep an audit log as you go. Write down what you noticed and where, even if you are not yet sure it is a problem. In the next session you will turn those notes into findings, and in the project you will need the evidence.
study.example: The stated purpose is 'assign students to after-school clubs'. A column called inferred_income_band has nothing to do with that purpose, so it should already be on your list before you look at a single value.

No account or sign-in is needed. The viewer is built into the portal and the CSV opens in any spreadsheet.

sessions.title: Find what is wrong
sessions.intro: Turn your first look into a findings table. Every finding names a place in the data, a type of problem, and what you saw.

study.title: Six kinds of data problem
body: Missing values are blanks where a value should be. Inconsistent formats are the same fact written different ways, such as 2026-09-03 and 03/09/2026, or TY and Transition Year. A computer treats these as different values, so counts and groupings go wrong. Duplicates are the same record more than once, sometimes with small differences in capitalisation that hide them from a simple check.

Sensitive or unnecessary fields are columns the purpose does not need, or that could cause harm if leaked or misused: home addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and above all guesses about people. Suspicious values are ones that cannot be true, like an attendance of 104 percent, and they usually point to a bug in how the data was collected.

Imbalance or bias is the quiet one. If almost everyone in the Coding club is one gender, or nearly every row is from one year group, a model trained on this data will learn that pattern and repeat it in its recommendations. The data is not wrong, exactly; it just does not represent everyone fairly, and the model cannot tell the difference.
study.example: Finding: column signup_date, Inconsistent format, 'three different date styles in the same column, so sorting by date would be wrong'. That is a target, an issue type and a note: enough for someone else to check it.

activity.instructions: Work through the table and the column summary. Add at least five findings covering at least three different issue types. Click a column header or a row number to fill in the target, choose the issue type, and write a note someone else could check.

sessions.reflection: Which of your findings would do the most damage if nobody caught it before the app was built, and why?

sessions.title: Propose the fix
sessions.intro: For every finding there is a choice: fix it, flag it, remove it, or collect it differently next time.

study.title: Fix, flag, remove, or collect differently
body: Some problems can be fixed in the data itself: pick one date format and convert the others, choose one spelling of the year group, remove exact duplicates. Write down every rule you apply so someone can repeat it and so nobody thinks the cleaned file is the original.

Some problems cannot be fixed by an analyst. A blank club choice cannot be invented; the honest options are to flag the row, go back and ask, or leave it out and say so. A value like -5 percent attendance should be flagged, not quietly changed to 5, because you do not know what really happened.

Some columns should simply be removed for this purpose: an inferred income band was never collected from anyone and cannot be checked, and a free-text notes column full of opinions about students is both unfair and unnecessary. Finally, some problems are about collection, not cleaning. An imbalance in who signed up for Coding is not solved by editing rows; it is solved by asking why, and by changing how the club is promoted or how sign-ups are gathered.
study.example: Cleaning rule: 'year_group: map TY, ty, 4 and Transition Year to TY'. Collection change: 'ask for club choice with a required drop-down instead of a free text box, so it cannot be left blank or misspelt'.

activity.title: Cleaning and collection plan
activity.instructions: Write your plan so that another analyst could carry it out without asking you questions.
fields: Problems I would fix in the data, and the exact rule for each…
Problems I would flag or leave out rather than fix, and why…
Columns I would remove for this purpose, and why…
One change to how the data is collected next time…

downloads.label: Cleaned dataset template (CSV)
downloads.note: The same columns minus the five sensitive or unnecessary ones, with empty rows. Use it if you would rather clean the data in a spreadsheet.

sessions.reflection: Which of your fixes could itself introduce a new error or unfairness if done carelessly?

sessions.title: Responsible Data Card
sessions.intro: Publish a short, honest card that travels with the dataset and tells the next person what it can and cannot be trusted for.

study.title: A data card is a warning label and a promise
body: A Responsible Data Card is a one-page description that travels with a dataset. It states the purpose, lists what is collected, says how each field was obtained (volunteered, observed or inferred), and names who could be harmed if the data is wrong, leaked, or used for something else.

It also records what you did: what was removed, what was fixed and how, what was flagged and left alone. Anyone who trains a model on the data later can read the card and know its limits instead of discovering them in the model's mistakes.

The most important line on the card is what the data must not be used for. Club sign-up data collected to run clubs must not be used to rank students, to guess family income, or to contact parents about anything else. Writing that down is how a purpose stays a purpose.
study.example: 'Must not be used for: predicting which students are likely to drop out. The data contains attendance and free-text notes that were never checked and would make that prediction unfair.'

activity.title: Responsible Data Card
activity.instructions: Complete the six sections. Be specific: name columns, numbers and people affected, not general statements.
fields: Purpose: what this dataset is for…
What is collected: the columns kept, in plain words…
Volunteered, observed or inferred: how each kept field was obtained…
Who could be harmed, and how…
What was removed or fixed, and the rules used…
What the data must not be used for…
